newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds rise; but dollar weakens.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds rise; but dollar weakens.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks rose on Friday, chalking up their biggest weekly gain ever on strong corporate earnings.
Bonds also strengthened, but the dollar fell.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended 44.95 points higher at 6,703.55 -- gaining 311.86 points from last Friday's close as the blue-chip market clawed back from a four-week sell-off of 700 points.
The weekly gain was the biggest ever for the 30-stock Dow, beating the 206-point surge in the week of Aug. 2 last year.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,499 to 924 on active volume of 468 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The Nasdaq Composite index also finished higher, gaining 5.50 points to 1,222.57, following strong gains in Microsoft Corp. one day after the company posted much stronger-than-expected fiscal third quarter earnings.
Even as the Dow continued to undo the damage from its month-long slide, analysts were reluctant to predict clear sailing for the market.

"We saw some good bargain-hunting this week, but overall the market was quite mixed," said Eugene Peroni, chief technical analyst with Janney, Montgomery Scott. "I would view this week as an impressive reaction to an oversold market."

Analysts said the relatively strong showings by sectors typically viewed as defensive investments, such as oil and consumer products companies, was evidence of a market still tentative after its recent declines.

"The rally has been fairly narrow, which disturbs us a bit," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker. "This market has to rotate and the cyclicals are going to have to emerge as leadership for this market to get its next leg up."
The narrowness of the rally was most evident among Nasdaq stocks, which managed only modest gains despite Microsoft's stellar 9-1/2 point rally to 107-5/8.

"Point for point, the statistics may show this was one of the best weeks for some of the averages," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "But this wasn't a case where a rising tide lifted all the ships."
The 30-year Treasury bond rose 5/32, or $1.56 per $1,000 face value, lowering its yield to 7.05 percent from Thursday's close of 7.07 percent. The price and yield move in opposite directions.
Late Friday, the dollar settled at 1.7118 German marks, down from 1.7238 marks late Thursday. The dollar fell to 125.88 Japanese yen from 125.98 yen.
Wheat prices soared to 10-month highs as worries about potential poor crops in the United States and Europe gripped the market.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for May delivery closed 11-3/4 cents a bushel higher at $4.37 after hitting a high of $4.38, the highest level since May 28.
At the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee prices rose for the third day on worries about tight stocks. Coffee for May delivery closed up 6.75 cents at 216.55 cents a pound.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index closed up 11.6 points at 4,310.5, for a net gain of just 39.8 points for the week. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average climbed 258.73 points or 1.43 percent to end at 18,352.14, a rise of 505.16 from seven days ago.
